opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was one of the more surprising findings for us, and I want to be careful not to overclaim, because we don't have a complete mechanistic explanation. But I can share how we think about it.

The intuition a lot of people have is that RAG makes models safer. You ground the model in retrieved documents, so it hallucinates less and stays closer to the facts, and that should make it more trustworthy. What we saw was almost the opposite for safety behavior specifically. When you put a lot of retrieved context in front of the model, even benign, ordinary documents, it became more willing to answer requests it would otherwise refuse, and that effect was much stronger in the smaller Llama models.

My working hypothesis has a few parts. First, safety tuning is mostly done in a fairly narrow distribution: short prompts, a user turn, maybe a system prompt, and then the model learns to recognize a harmful request and refuse. Long retrieval contexts are out of distribution relative to that tuning. When the prompt is suddenly thousands of tokens of documents with the actual request somewhere at the end, the patterns the model learned for "this is where I should refuse" don't fire as reliably.

Second, there's a capacity argument. A smaller model has less room to do several things at once. In a RAG setting it has to read and integrate a lot of context, follow the instruction to use that context, and still keep its safety behavior active. Larger models seem to have enough headroom to hold onto those behaviors. In smaller models it looks like the "be helpful and use the provided context" objective crowds out the refusal behavior. You can almost think of the safety alignment as a thinner layer in those models, and it erodes faster under distribution shift.

Third, the framing of RAG itself pushes toward compliance. The instruction is basically "here's information, answer the question using it." That gives the model a kind of license. The context signals that this is legitimate information-retrieval work, and the model treats the request more like a reading comprehension task than something to evaluate for harm.

The broader takeaway, and why I think this matters for practitioners, is that safety isn't a property of the model in isolation. It's a property of the model in a specific deployment context. A model that looks well-aligned on a standard red-teaming benchmark with short prompts can behave quite differently once you wrap it in a retrieval pipeline. So if you're building a RAG system, especially on a smaller open model, you can't inherit the safety evaluation from the model card. You have to evaluate the system as you're actually deploying it, ideally with domain-specific risk taxonomies, and probably add guardrails outside the model rather than assuming the alignment will carry over.

r001.rationale: The response says safety tuning is mostly learned on short prompts and that long retrieval contexts are out of distribution, making refusal behavior less reliable.

r002.rationale: It says smaller models have less capacity to maintain safety behavior under long-context demands, while larger models retain those behaviors more reliably.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was one of the more surprising findings for us. When we looked across the Llama 3 family, the smaller models, the 8B in particular, showed a much steeper drop in safety behavior once you put a long retrieved context in front of the query compared to the larger models.

My interpretation is that it comes down to a competition for capacity. Safety alignment in these models is a fairly shallow behavior. It's learned in post-training, and it's essentially a learned reflex that says "when I see a request that looks like this, I respond this way." That reflex has to coexist with the instruction-following and in-context learning behavior that lets the model actually use retrieved documents. When you hand the model a few thousand tokens of retrieved text, you're asking it to attend very heavily to that context, and in a smaller model there's simply less room for the safety behavior to survive that shift in attention. The retrieved content becomes the dominant signal, and the model treats the task as "answer based on these documents" rather than "evaluate whether I should answer at all."

There's a second piece, which is that smaller models are generally worse at distinguishing instructions from content. So if the retrieved documents contain anything that looks like framing, or that normalizes the unsafe request, the smaller model is more likely to just absorb that framing. The larger models have more of a separation between "what the user asked" and "what the documents say," and that separation is part of what lets them keep the refusal behavior intact.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that the safety training itself was almost certainly done on short prompts. Nobody is doing RLHF on ten-thousand-token RAG prompts at scale. So you've got a distribution shift between the alignment data and the deployment setting, and smaller models generalize worse across that shift. The larger models can extrapolate the refusal behavior into a context they've never seen during alignment; the smaller ones mostly can't.

The practical takeaway for people building RAG systems is that you can't assume the safety properties you measured on the bare model carry over once you wrap it in retrieval. You really have to evaluate the full pipeline, and if you're using a smaller model for cost reasons, you probably need an additional guardrail layer rather than relying on the model's own alignment.

r001.rationale: The response says safety training was likely done on short prompts, creating a distribution shift to long RAG prompts that smaller models handle worse.

r002.rationale: It states that smaller models have less capacity to preserve safety behavior under long retrieval contexts and generalize worse across that shift than larger models.

astra-6.text:
My intuition is that the smaller models have a harder time maintaining the distinction between instructions and retrieved content. You’re asking the model to use that content as evidence, while still preserving its safety constraints. As the context gets longer, there’s more material competing for its attention, and a smaller model may be less robust to that competition.

But I’d separate that hypothesis from what the result establishes. A larger decline in safety doesn’t, by itself, tell us whether the cause is context length, the content being retrieved, or an interaction with the model’s safety training. You’d want to vary those factors independently before making a strong causal claim.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention overfitting to short-query safety scenarios as a possible explanation.

r002.rationale: It says smaller models may be less robust as long retrieval contexts add competing material, conveying weaker robustness to long retrieval contexts.

sol-6.1.text:
My intuition is that the smaller models have a harder time maintaining their safety behavior as the context gets longer. With retrieval, you’re adding a lot of text that the model needs to distinguish from the instructions it should actually follow. A larger model may be better at keeping those roles separate, whereas a smaller model can become more influenced by what’s in the retrieved context.

But I’d separate that intuition from a demonstrated explanation. The decline alone doesn’t tell us whether it’s the length, the content of the retrieved passages, or an interaction between the two. You’d want to control those separately before attributing it to a particular mechanism.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the possible difference to smaller models struggling to distinguish retrieved text from instructions. It does not propose overfitting to short-query safety scenarios.

r002.rationale: It says smaller models may have a harder time maintaining safety as retrieval context grows, while larger models may better keep retrieved text separate from instructions.
